title: High Turnout Unseats Incumbents in Serbia, Brazil and US Elections
excerpt: Student List ends 14 years of SNS rule in Serbia, Lula overturns a first-round deficit for a fourth term in Brazil, and US midterms post the second-highest turnout since 1914 as Democrats take Congress.
body:
• Serbia's student-backed Student List won the October 25 snap election with about 53% of the vote, ending 14 years of Serbian Progressive Party rule, according to the Jamestown Foundation and Reuters reporting.
  • In Brazil, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in the runoff with 51.8% to Flavio Bolsonaro's 48.2%, overturning a 2.2 million-vote first-round deficit as close to three million more people voted in the second round.
  • In the United States, preliminary University of Florida Election Lab data put midterm turnout at 49.42% of eligible voters — about 124.3 million ballots, the second-highest midterm rate since 1914 — and Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.
  • For readers in the US, the new Congress takes office in January, so the midterm result, not the campaign, is what will shape federal legislation for the next two years; final US totals are still preliminary and will change as late mail and provisional ballots are certified.

Three elections, one pattern: more voters, weaker incumbents

Within ten days, voters in Serbia, Brazil and the United States turned out in unusually large numbers — and in each case the larger electorate hurt the side that had held power. The results were reported separately by election commissions and news organisations in each country, not as a coordinated movement. What links them is arithmetic: when participation rose, long-dominant parties and incumbents lost ground they had held in lower-turnout contests.

Serbia: students turn a protest into a majority

Serbia's Student List won the October 25 snap parliamentary elections with about 53 percent of the vote, according to the Jamestown Foundation's analysis of the result. Reuters, reporting with almost 99 percent of votes counted, put the students' candidates at 52.7 percent against 39.2 percent for Aleksandar Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party-led alliance, giving the Student List 139 seats in the 250-seat parliament against 97 for the SNS alliance.

Vucic, who had dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014, conceded defeat on election night. Serbian turnout was nearly 69 percent, according to The Conclave's analysis. The movement behind the list grew out of protests after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, which killed 16 people and triggered two years of anti-corruption demonstrations, according to both Jamestown and Reuters. Its candidates are mostly academics and other newcomers selected by student assemblies, and it has not yet named a prime minister; cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic heads its candidate list.

Brazil: Lula comes from behind in the runoff

In Brazil, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro 51.8 percent to 48.2 percent in the presidential runoff and was elected to a fourth term, the London Review of Books reported. Lula won 64.2 million votes — over ten million more than in the first round.

The comeback is the factual core of the story. Lula trailed by 2.2 million votes in the first round, then won the runoff by more than 4.4 million. Turnout made a difference, the LRB noted: close to three million more people voted in the second round, with large gains for Lula in the northeast, Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. Flavio Bolsonaro has disputed the process, according to reporting summarised by The Conclave, while his Liberal Party recognised the outcome.

United States: second-highest midterm turnout in a century

The same pattern reached the United States on November 3. A preliminary estimate compiled by The World Data from University of Florida Election Lab figures puts turnout at 49.42 percent of eligible voters, or about 124.3 million ballots — second only to 2018's 50.05 percent among midterms since 1914, and above 2022's 46.1 percent. More than 60 million ballots were cast before Election Day, a midterm record. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, according to the same reporting.

Israel completes the picture — with a harder result

The Conclave's survey also covered Israel's October 27 parliamentary election, where it reported the ruling bloc won 53 seats and the opposition bloc 48, with 19 seats held by Arab parties — leaving government formation dependent on parties both leaders had pledged not to deal with. It reported Arab voter participation rising sharply. Unlike Serbia, Brazil and the US, Israel produced no clean transfer of power, only a cliffhanger that President Isaac Herzog must now try to resolve through consultations.

What to watch next

In Serbia, the Student List must form a government — parliament must convene within 30 days of final results and a government within 90 days after that, according to Jamestown. In Brazil, Lula begins his new term on January 5, 2027. In the US, certified totals will confirm the preliminary picture.
